title: Li, ritual courtesy
hookLine: Confucian ritual and courtesy shape the heart through the body

lines: SHE DOESN'T FEEL IT. SHE SAYS IT.
CAN THE HANDS LEAD THE HEART?
cards: A small girl gets a present from her aunt. It's socks. Her face falls.
Her father leans down and whispers: say thank you. She doesn't feel thankful. She says it anyway, a little sulky.
Fake, maybe. But over the years she keeps saying it, and slowly the words reach inward. One day, without noticing, she means it.

Which came first, the thanks or the thankfulness? One hunch says the heart has to change first, and the manners follow. Confucian teaching opens another possibility: the hands and the mouth can help lead the heart.

teach.b: The word is li. It can be translated ritual, propriety or courtesy, and it covers all three. Li is the great ceremonies, the offerings, the mourning rites.
It's also how you bow, greet an elder, hand someone a cup. In the Analects, Confucius's student Yan Yuan asks him about ren, true goodness.
The answer, in Legge's translation: "To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue." Then Confucius makes it concrete.
In paraphrase: look at nothing, listen to nothing, say nothing, do nothing that is against li. It sounds rigid. It isn't meant to be empty.
Another student asks what the root of li is, and Confucius praises the question.

teach.h: THE ROOT: REAL GRIEF OVER PERFECT DETAIL.
teach.b: His answer, in paraphrase: in ceremonies, simple is better than lavish; at a funeral, real grief matters more than getting every detail right.
Elsewhere he asks, more or less, what use is ritual to someone with no goodness in them? So li without a heart is hollow.

teach.h: THE HEART IS TRAINED THROUGH THE FORM.
teach.b: But Confucian teachers read the form this way: the heart is trained through it. You bow, and the bow teaches respect. You stand when an elder enters, and standing makes room in you for them.

teach.h: TO SUBDUE ONE'S SELF AND RETURN TO PROPRIETY.
teach.b: Courtesy isn't a mask over who you are. Done again and again, carefully, it shapes who you become.

This week's days share that thread: hymns sung, a sangat side by side, Yan Hui's sitting, the slow arms of qigong, tai chi's turning weight, Zengzi's questions. Put the body somewhere good, and the heart tends to follow.

how: In Confucian tradition li runs from formal rites, such as honoring ancestors and mourning, to everyday courtesy, such as greeting elders, bowing, and offering things with both hands, practiced so that respect becomes second nature.

an inner feeling that must come before any outward act
ritual, propriety and courtesy, forms that shape the heart

make the ceremony as grand as you can afford.
games.why: Confucius praises the question, then puts sincerity at the root: simple over lavish, real grief over minute correctness.

practice: Choose one small courtesy, a greeting, a thank you, handing someone something with both hands, and rehearse it slowly in your mind: the person, your face, your hands, your voice, unhurried.
Feel what it would be like to mean it fully; if you don't yet, that's fine, the form is allowed to go first.

wordCard.voice: Li. Ritual, propriety, courtesy, in the Confucian tradition: forms of the body that, done with care, shape the heart. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: courtesy shapes. The thanks can come before the thankfulness does. Another week walked.
